claim: Shape perception is considered a function of the ventral visual pathway.
source: Although shape perception is considered a function of the ventral visual pathway, evidence suggests that the dorsal pathway also derives shape-based representations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Evidence suggests that the dorsal pathway also derives shape-based representations.
source: Although shape perception is considered a function of the ventral visual pathway, evidence suggests that the dorsal pathway also derives shape-based representations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: In both pathways, shape sensitivity increased from early visual cortex to extrastriate cortex but then decreased in anterior regions.
source: In both pathways, shape sensitivity increased from early visual cortex to extrastriate cortex but then decreased in anterior regions.
evidence: This finding is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the voxel-wise analysis and piecewise regression results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The lateral aspect of the ventral pathway and posterior regions of the dorsal pathway were sensitive to the availability of fundamental shape properties, even for unrecognizable images.
source: Moreover, the lateral aspect of the ventral pathway and posterior regions of the dorsal pathway were sensitive to the availability of fundamental shape properties, even for unrecognizable images.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment results.

claim: The representational similarity between the posterior-dorsal and lateral-ventral regions was corroborated by a multivariate analysis.
source: This apparent representational similarity between the posterior-dorsal and lateral-ventral regions was corroborated by a multivariate analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the RSA analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The activation profile of posterior dorsal regions was correlated with recognition performance.
source: Finally, as with ventral pathway, the activation profile of posterior dorsal regions was correlated with recognition performance, suggesting a possible contribution to perception.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Shape is the most fundamental perceived property of objects.
source: Shape is the most fundamental perceived property of objects, and, accordingly, shape processing is crucial for successful visual object recognition (Palmer, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Palmer, 1999.

claim: Shape processing is crucial for successful visual object recognition.
source: Shape is the most fundamental perceived property of objects, and, accordingly, shape processing is crucial for successful visual object recognition (Palmer, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Palmer, 1999.

claim: Deriving information about the shapes of objects in the input has long been considered to be under the purview of the ventral visual pathway.
source: Deriving information about the shapes of objects in the input has long been considered to be under the purview of the ventral visual pathway (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982) and many functional imaging studies have provided evidence to support this claim (e.g., Freud et al., 2013; Grill-Spector et al., 1998; Kourtzi and Kanwisher, 2000; Lerner et al., 2001; Malach et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a gradient of shape sensitivity in the ventral pathway, with posterior regions in the early to mid-visual cortex being less responsive to the shape of the object than more anterior regions.
source: Specifically, these investigations have uncovered a gradient of shape sensitivity in the ventral pathway, with posterior regions in the early to mid-visual cortex (i.e., V1-hV4) being less responsive to the shape of the object than more anterior regions, such as the Lateral Occipital Cortex (LOC) and the Fusiform Gyrus (FG).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Shape sensitivity in anterior regions of the ventral pathway is correlated with perceptual abilities.
source: Additionally, shape sensitivity in these latter, anterior regions is correlated with perceptual abilities, and a lesion to these areas results in an impairment in object perception (e.g., Freud et al., 2017a; Goodale et al., 1991; Konen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A lesion to anterior regions of the ventral pathway results in an impairment in object perception.
source: Additionally, shape sensitivity in these latter, anterior regions is correlated with perceptual abilities, and a lesion to these areas results in an impairment in object perception (e.g., Freud et al., 2017a; Goodale et al., 1991; Konen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies have uncovered object representations mediated by the dorsal pathway, even under conditions in which no visuomotor response is required.
source: Human neuroimaging studies (Freud et al., 2015; Jeong and Xu, 2016; Konen and Kastner, 2008; Zachariou et al., 2014; Zachariou et al., 2017; Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Bracci et al., 2017), primate electrophysiological studies (Durand et al., 2007; Janssen et al., 2008; Janssen et al., 2000; Van Dromme et al., 2016); for review see Theys et al., 2015), comparative studies between human and primates (Denys et al., 2004; Sawamura et al., 2005) and human neuropsychology (Freud et al., 2017a) have all uncovered object representations mediated by the dorsal pathway, even under conditions in which no visuomotor response is required.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The large-scale topographical organization of dorsal object representations obeys a spatial gradient in which posterior regions of the pathway derive shape representations and contribute to visual perception, whereas more anterior regions derive representations that are better tuned to subserve visuomotor behaviors.
source: We hypothesized that the large-scale topographical organization of dorsal object representations obeys a spatial gradient in which posterior regions of the pathway derive shape representations and contribute to visual perception, whereas more anterior regions derive representations that are better tuned to subserve visuomotor behaviors (Freud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is the hypothesis stated in the introduction and supported by the experimental results.

claim: The decrease in BOLD activation with increased scrambling serves as an index of shape sensitivity.
source: The decrease in BOLD activation with increased scrambling serves as an index of shape sensitivity (Denys et al., 2004; Grill-Spector et al., 1998; Lerner et al., 2001; Malach et al., 1995; Murray et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Box scrambling increases the number of edges.
source: First, it increases the number of edges, and early visual cortex is especially sensitive to this type of information (Grill-Spector et al., 1998; Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of the box scrambling method.

claim: Early visual cortex is especially sensitive to edges.
source: First, it increases the number of edges, and early visual cortex is especially sensitive to this type of information (Grill-Spector et al., 1998; Lerner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Box scrambling disrupts crucial shape attributes such as good continuation and figure-ground segregation.
source: Second, box scrambling disrupts crucial shape attributes such as good continuation and figure-ground segregation (Koffka, 1935; Qiu and von der Heydt, 2005; Read et al., 1997), and, unsurprisingly, eliminates the identity information of the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of the box scrambling method and supported by citations.

claim: Box scrambling eliminates the identity information of the stimulus.
source: Second, box scrambling disrupts crucial shape attributes such as good continuation and figure-ground segregation (Koffka, 1935; Qiu and von der Heydt, 2005; Read et al., 1997), and, unsurprisingly, eliminates the identity information of the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of the box scrambling method.

claim: Diffeomorphic scrambling increasingly precludes the identification of the object but preserves some fundamental shape properties.
source: To circumvent these limitations and verify the results, in the second experiment we used a diffeomorphic scrambling manipulation that increasingly precludes the identification of the object but preserves some fundamental shape properties by repeatedly applying a flow field generated from a set of two-dimensional cosine components with random phase and amplitude (Stojanoski and Cusack, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: In the ventral pathway, a negative slope was found in the vicinity of the calcarine sulcus and in the posterior occipital lobe more generally.
source: In the ventral pathway (Figure 2A), a negative slope was found in the vicinity of the calcarine sulcus and in the posterior occipital lobe more generally, and likely reflects the sensitivity of early visual cortex to edges and high spatial frequency information in the input (Lerner et al., 2001); for an additional interpretation, see Murray et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The negative slope in early visual cortex likely reflects the sensitivity of early visual cortex to edges and high spatial frequency information in the input.
source: In the ventral pathway (Figure 2A), a negative slope was found in the vicinity of the calcarine sulcus and in the posterior occipital lobe more generally, and likely reflects the sensitivity of early visual cortex to edges and high spatial frequency information in the input (Lerner et al., 2001); for an additional interpretation, see Murray et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: In more anterior regions of the ventral pathway, a positive slope was evident both on the lateral and the inferior surface of the occipitotemporal cortex.
source: In more anterior regions of the ventral pathway, a positive slope was evident both on the lateral and the inferior surface of the occipitotemporal cortex (i.e., LO, Parahippocampal gyrus and Fusiform gyrus).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In even more anterior regions of the ventral pathway, a decrease in shape sensitivity was detected.
source: However, in even more anterior regions (i.e., anterior and medial temporal cortex), a decrease in shape sensitivity was detected.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The piecewise regression revealed that the data were well described by two linear components in the ventral pathway.
source: The piecewise regression revealed that the data were well described by two linear components.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The first component in the ventral pathway reflected the increase in shape sensitivity in the transition between early visual cortex and object-selective cortex and was characterized by a positive correlation between slope and location on the posterior-anterior axis.
source: The first component reflected the increase in shape sensitivity in the transition between early visual cortex and object-selective cortex and was characterized by a positive correlation between slope and location on the posterior-anterior axis [LH: t(10)=8.21, q < 0.00001 CI {0.39, 0.69}; RH: t(10)=12.1 q < 0.00001, CI {0.43, 0.62}].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The second component in the ventral pathway was characterized by a decrease in shape sensitivity, as evident from the negative correlation between location on the posterior-anterior axis and slope.
source: The second component was characterized by a decrease in shape sensitivity, as evident from the negative correlation between location on the posterior-anterior axis and slope [LH: t(10)=9.5, q = 0.00001, CI{−0.32, −0.51}; RH: t(10)=6.94, q = 0.00001, CI {−0.20 −0.39}; Figure 2B].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The robust positive first component in the ventral pathway is consistent with previous investigations of the ventral pathway.
source: The robust positive first component is consistent with previous investigations of the ventral pathway (Lerner et al., 2001; Murray et al., 2002), and replicates the hierarchical nature of shape processing in which more elaborate and complex representations are derived as one moves rostrally (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: The reduction in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the temporal lobe might reflect a transition to more semantic and memory-based representation.
source: The reduction in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the temporal lobe might reflect a transition to more semantic and memory-based representation (Kravitz et al., 2013; Visser et al., 2010), rather than shape sensitivity per se, but might also be a consequence of MRI distortion effects which are more common in these regions (Olman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a possible interpretation and supported by citations.

claim: Shape sensitivity in the dorsal pathway was not evident in early visual areas, but emerged in extrastriate occipital cortex and reached a peak in the posterior intraparietal sulcus.
source: As in the ventral pathway, shape sensitivity in the dorsal pathway was not evident in early visual areas, but emerged in extrastriate occipital cortex and reached a peak in the posterior intraparietal sulcus (IPS).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The piecewise regression in the dorsal pathway revealed a positive correlation for the first component, which reflects the increase in shape sensitivity.
source: Accordingly, the piecewise regression revealed a positive correlation for the first component, which reflects the increase in shape sensitivity [LH: t(10)=5.15, q = 0.0004 CI {0.32, 0.82}; RH: t(10)=10, q = 0.00001, CI {0.62, 0.97}], and a robust negative correlation for the second component, which reflects the decrease in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the dorsal pathway [LH: t(10)=8.54, q = 0.00001 CI {−0.32, −0.55}; RH: t(10)=8.94, q = 0.000001, CI {−0.34, −0.57}; Figure 2C].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The piecewise regression in the dorsal pathway revealed a robust negative correlation for the second component, which reflects the decrease in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the dorsal pathway.
source: Accordingly, the piecewise regression revealed a positive correlation for the first component, which reflects the increase in shape sensitivity [LH: t(10)=5.15, q = 0.0004 CI {0.32, 0.82}; RH: t(10)=10, q = 0.00001, CI {0.62, 0.97}], and a robust negative correlation for the second component, which reflects the decrease in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the dorsal pathway [LH: t(10)=8.54, q = 0.00001 CI {−0.32, −0.55}; RH: t(10)=8.94, q = 0.000001, CI {−0.34, −0.57}; Figure 2C].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The two pathways have similar topographical organization.
source: The key finding here is that the two pathways have similar topographical organization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the data from both pathways.

claim: Object representations in the dorsal pathway are not monolithic but differ qualitatively along the posterior-anterior axis.
source: In addition, these findings provide novel evidence for the nature of shape processing in the dorsal pathway and indicate that object representations in this pathway are not monolithic but, rather, differ qualitatively along the posterior-anterior axis (Freud et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the data showing different shape sensitivity along the axis.

claim: The maximal shape sensitivity was more posterior in the dorsal relative to the ventral pathway.
source: In particular, the maximal shape sensitivity (the apex or inflection point of the regression line) was more posterior in the dorsal relative to the ventral pathway [F(1,10) = 22.11, p=0.0008, ηp2 = 0.68, CI {12 21}; Figure 2D].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The average sensitivity of all shape-selective voxels was significantly greater in the ventral than dorsal pathway.
source: Additionally, the average sensitivity of all shape-selective voxels (slope > 0) was significantly greater in the ventral than dorsal pathway [F(1,10) = 45, p=0.00005, ηp2 = 0.81, CI {0.01 0.02}; Figure 2E].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There was an interaction between pathway and hemisphere, with greater difference between the pathways in the left than the right hemisphere.
source: Interestingly, this main effect was modulated by an interaction with hemisphere [F(1,10) = 11.37, p=0.007, ηp2 = 0.53, CI {0.01 0.02}] with greater difference between the pathways in the left than the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The greater difference between the pathways in shape sensitivity in the left hemisphere might reflect hemispheric specialization, such that the left dorsal pathway is more tuned to visuomotor aspects than the right dorsal pathway.
source: The greater difference between the pathways in shape sensitivity in the left hemisphere might reflect hemispheric specialization, such that the left dorsal pathway is more tuned to visuomotor aspects than the right dorsal pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a possible interpretation.

claim: In the ventral pathway, the piecewise regression in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment revealed a positive correlation between slope and location on the posterior-anterior axis (first component).
source: In the ventral pathway, the piecewise regression revealed a positive correlation between slope and location on the posterior-anterior axis (first component), which reflects the emergence of shape sensitivity in the transition from early visual cortex to object selective cortex [LH: t(10)=25.2 q<0.0000001, CI [0.59, 0.70]; RH: t(10)=13.2, q = 0.000004, CI {44, 0.63}], and a negative correlation for the second component, which reflects the decrease in shape sensitivity in the most anterior parts of the temporal lobe [LH: t(10)= 9.77, q = 0.0000005, CI{−0.25, −0.40}; RH: t(10)=4.57, q = 0.001, CI{−0.09, −0.27}].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In the ventral pathway, the piecewise regression in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment revealed a negative correlation for the second component, which reflects the decrease in shape sensitivity in the most anterior parts of the temporal lobe.
source: In the ventral pathway, the piecewise regression revealed a positive correlation between slope and location on the posterior-anterior axis (first component), which reflects the emergence of shape sensitivity in the transition from early visual cortex to object selective cortex [LH: t(10)=25.2 q<0.0000001, CI [0.59, 0.70]; RH: t(10)=13.2, q = 0.000004, CI {44, 0.63}], and a negative correlation for the second component, which reflects the decrease in shape sensitivity in the most anterior parts of the temporal lobe [LH: t(10)= 9.77, q = 0.0000005, CI{−0.25, −0.40}; RH: t(10)=4.57, q = 0.001, CI{−0.09, −0.27}].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: On the lateral surface of the ventral pathway, a flatter slope was found in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, suggesting that this region was less sensitive to the diffeomorphic manipulation than to the box scrambling manipulation.
source: Interestingly, however, on the lateral surface of the ventral pathway (corresponding to LOC, see also ROI analysis, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), a flatter slope was found (i.e., similar activation to the different levels of image distortion), suggesting that this region was less sensitive to the diffeomorphic manipulation than to the box scrambling manipulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: LOC appears to represent the presence of a well-defined shape, with clear contours, rather than a representation of the object's identity.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Malach et al., 1995; Margalit et al., 2016), LOC appears to represent the presence of a well-defined shape, with clear contours, rather than a representation of the object's identity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The piecewise regression of the dorsal pathway in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment revealed two opposite linear components.
source: The piecewise regression of the dorsal pathway revealed two opposite linear components.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The first component in the dorsal pathway in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment was characterized by a positive correlation between slope and location on the y-axis, which reflects the transition from early visual cortex to object-selective cortex.
source: The first component was characterized by a positive correlation between slope and location on the y-axis, which reflects the transition from early visual cortex to object-selective cortex [LH: t (10)=3.98, q = 0.002, CI {0.22, 0.80}; RH: t (10)=7.31, q = 0.00005, CI{43, 0.81}].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The second component in the dorsal pathway in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment was characterized by a negative correlation between slope and location of the voxels on the posterior-anterior axis.
source: In contrast, the second component, which reflects the representational gradient along the IPS, was characterized by a negative correlation between slope and location of the voxels on the posterior-anterior axis [LH: t (10)=5.96, q = 0.0001, CI {−0.16, −0.35}; RH: t (10)=6.39, q = 0.0001, CI{−0.19, −0.39}].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Despite the difference in the overall shape sensitivity between the two experiments, they provided consistent information on the overall large-scale organization of shape sensitivity.
source: A repeated measures ANOVA on the correlation values (between slope and location of voxels on the y-axis), with Experiment as a between-subjects variable, and pathway, component and hemisphere as within-subject variables, revealed no interactions between Experiment and the other variables [all ps > 0.05]. This result indicates that, despite the difference in the overall shape sensitivity between the two experiments, they provided consistent information on the overall large-scale organization of shape sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The maximal shape sensitivity emerged in more posterior regions of the dorsal pathway compared with the ventral pathway in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment.
source: As in box scrambling experiment, the maximal shape sensitivity emerged in more posterior regions of the dorsal pathway compared with the ventral pathway [F (1,10)=18.78, p=0.001, ηp2 = 0.65], and the effect held when distance based on the Y and Z axes served as the dependent variable [F (1,10)=45, p=0.00005, ηp2 = 0.81].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The inflection point of the regression was more anterior in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment compared with box scrambling experiment.
source: Interestingly, the inflection point of the regression was more anterior in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment compared with box scrambling experiment [F (1,20)=8.45, p=0.008, ηp2 = 0.29], and this might reflect the increased high-level shape or identity processing associated with the diffeomorphic scrambling stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The average shape sensitivity was greater in the ventral than the dorsal pathway in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment.
source: In addition, we compared the overall neural sensitivity to shape information in all shape-selective voxels (slope > 0). The average shape sensitivity was greater in the ventral than the dorsal pathway [F (1,10)=37, p=0.0001, ηp2 = 0.79].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Shape sensitivity was greater overall in the ventral than dorsal pathway across the two experiments.
source: The comparison between the two experiments revealed two main effects, with no interaction. As expected, there was a main effect of pathway: shape sensitivity was greater overall in the ventral than dorsal pathway across the two experiments [F (1,20)=83, p=0.000001, ηp2 = 0.8].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a main effect of Experiment, with greater average positive slope in the box scrambling experiment than the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment.
source: There was also an additional main effect of Experiment, with greater average positive slope in the box scrambling experiment than the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, reflecting the different nature of the two manipulations [F (1,20)=32, p=0.00001, ηp2 = 0.62; see also Figure 1].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: An interaction between pathway and hemisphere was found and was not modulated by experiment.
source: Notably, an interaction between pathway and hemisphere [F (1,20)=10.85, p=0.003, ηp2 = 0.35] was found and was not modulated by experiment [F (1,20)<1].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction between pathway and hemisphere was the result of a greater difference between the two pathways in the left than right hemisphere.
source: This interaction was the result of a greater difference between the two pathways in the left than right hemisphere, and therefore further implicates hemispheric differences in shape processing.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Both early visual cortices and object-selective cortices were correlated with the shape model in the box scrambling experiment.
source: The results of the RSA are depicted in Figure 4B. Both early visual cortices and object-selective cortices were correlated with the shape model.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The correlation of early visual cortices to the shape model can be explained by the negative slope observed in those regions that carry information about the presence/absence of a shape and about low-level similarities.
source: The correlation of early visual cortices to the shape model can be explained by the negative slope observed in those regions that carry information about the presence/absence of a shape and about low-level similarities (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Mid-posterior parts of the dorsal pathway and ventral pathways were highly correlated with the shape sensitivity model.
source: More importantly, and compatible with the univariate analysis, mid-posterior parts of the dorsal pathway and ventral pathways were highly correlated with the shape sensitivity model, and this sensitivity decreased in more anterior parts of the parietal cortex and temporal lobe.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The patterns of activation in the posterior parts of the dorsal pathway were highly correlated with regions of the lateral ventral pathway.
source: In particular, the patterns of activation in the posterior parts of the dorsal pathway (i.e. V3a-IPS1) were highly correlated with regions of the lateral ventral pathway (i.e., LO1, LO2, and TO1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The between-pathways correlations were higher than the within-pathway correlations both in the ventral and dorsal pathways in the box scrambling experiment.
source: Interestingly, this analysis revealed that the between-pathways correlations were higher than the within-pathway correlations both in the ventral [F (1,10)=26.1, p=0.0004, ηp2 = 0.72,, CI{0.05, 0.13}] and dorsal [F (1,10)=19.3, p=0.001, ηp2 = 0.65, CI{0.05, 0.16}] pathways, further challenging a binary distinction between the two pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Regions in the dorsal and ventral pathway share highly similar representational structures based on the availability of shape information.
source: The RSA results converge with the univariate results and demonstrate that regions in the dorsal and ventral pathway share highly similar representational structures based on the availability of shape information, thereby challenging the binary distinction between the two pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the RSA analysis.

claim: Both early visual cortices and object-selective cortices were correlated with the shape model in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, however, these correlations were significantly reduced in comparison to the box scrambling experiment.
source: The results of the RSA are depicted in Figure 5B. Both early visual cortices and object-selective cortices were correlated with the shape model, however, these correlations were significantly reduced in comparison to the box scrambling experiment (for a direct comparison see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduction in the correlation to the shape model in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment is not an artifact of noise in the data.
source: Importantly, this reduction is not an artifact of noise in the data as evident from the noise ceiling calculation (gray bars, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduction in the correlation to the shape model in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment is more likely related to the fact that the impact of shape distortion was reduced for the diffeomorphic stimuli.
source: The reduction in the correlation to the shape model is therefore more likely related to the fact that the impact of shape distortion was reduced for the diffeomorphic stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The large-scale organization of the dorsal pathway was replicated in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, as the highest correlations with the shape model were observed in V3a-b and IPS0.
source: Importantly however, the large-scale organization of the dorsal pathway (particularly in the right hemisphere) was replicated in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, as the highest correlations with the shape model were observed in V3a-b and IPS0.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A robust reduction in the correlation to the shape model was observed along the ventral pathway, particularly along its lateral surface in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment.
source: A robust reduction in the correlation to the shape model was observed along the ventral pathway, particularly along its lateral surface.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The robust decrease of correlation to the shape model in the lateral ventral pathway suggests that the LOC codes shape information rather than a high-level abstraction of the object's identity.
source: The robust decrease of correlation to the shape model, further suggests that the LOC codes shape information rather than a high-level abstraction of the object's identity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The patterns of activation in the posterior parts of the dorsal pathway were highly correlated with regions of the ventral pathway in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment.
source: The MDS plot shows that the patterns of activation in the posterior parts of the dorsal pathway (i.e. V3a-IPS1) were highly correlated with regions of the ventral pathway (e.g., LO), while more anterior parts of the two pathways had distinctive representational structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The statistical quantification of the second-order correlation in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment replicated the box scrambling experiment findings, with higher correlations of the between-pathways ROIs compared with the correlations of the within-pathways ROIs.
source: The statistical quantification replicated the box scrambling experiment findings, with higher correlations of the between-pathways ROIs (lateral-ventral and posterior-dorsal) compared with the correlations of the within-pathways ROIs [within ventral: F(1,10) = 54, p=0.00002, ηp2 = 0.84,, CI{0.08, 0.15}; within dorsal: F (1,10) = 130, p=0.000001, ηp2 = 0.94, CI{0.11, 0.17}].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Object recognition abilities decreased as a function of scrambling in the box scrambling experiment.
source: Object recognition abilities decreased as a function of scrambling, as revealed by a main effect of scrambling level in the repeated measures ANOVA [F(1,10) = 477, p=0.000001, ηp2 = 0.97], and a robust simple effect of the linear contrast [F(1,10) = 1634, p=0.000001] (Figure 5A, black line).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: fMRI activation along the ventral pathway was correlated with perceptual performance on both the inferior and lateral surfaces in the box scrambling experiment.
source: Consistent with previous reports, fMRI activation along the ventral pathway was correlated with perceptual performance on both the inferior and lateral surfaces (r > 0, q < 0.05; Figure 6B, black markers).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dorsal-pathway activation was correlated with perceptual behavior in multiple ROIs along the IPS in the box scrambling experiment.
source: The more novel finding is that dorsal-pathway activation was also correlated with perceptual behavior in multiple ROIs along the IPS (r > 0, q < 0.05; Figure 6B), suggesting a functional role for the dorsal pathway in visual perception.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Object recognition abilities decreased as a function of scrambling in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment.
source: In the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, object recognition abilities decreased as a function of scrambling, as revealed by a main effect of level of scrambling in the repeated measures ANOVA [F(1,9)=929, p=0.0000001, ηp2 = 0.99], and a robust simple effect of the linear contrast [F(1,9)=20596, p=0.0000001] (Figure 6A, gray line).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Recognition performance for the scrambled versions observed in the diffeomorphic scrambling were lower than those obtained for the box scrambling experiment.
source: Recognition performance for the scrambled versions (levels S2, S3 and S4) observed in the diffeomorphic scrambling were lower than those obtained for the box scrambling experiment, as evident from the interaction between experiment and level of scrambling [F(4,76)=71, p=0.0000001, ηp2 = 0.78] and the planned comparisons [Fs(1,19) > 5.7, p<0.05].
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The lower fMRI sensitivity to object shape in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment could not be related to superior recognizability of the distorted images in this experiment.
source: Hence, the lower fMRI sensitivity to object shape (i.e. flatter slope) in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment could not be related to superior recognizability of the distorted images in this experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The partial correlation between performance and fMRI signal in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment revealed a correlation between fMRI activation and perceptual performance on both the inferior and lateral surfaces of the ventral pathway.
source: As in the box scrambling experiment, the partial correlation between performance and fMRI signal, with the level of scrambling as a covariate, revealed a correlation between fMRI activation and perceptual performance on both the inferior and lateral surfaces of the ventral pathway (r > 0, q < 0.05; Figure 6B. gray markers).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, the coupling between behavioral performance and fMRI activity was apparent in different ROIs along the IPS.
source: Importantly, in this analysis, the coupling between behavioral performance and fMRI activity was also apparent in different ROIs along the IPS (r > 0, q < 0.05.; Figure 6B. gray markers).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The dorsal pathway is known to be highly responsive to images of tools, which convey visuomotor information.
source: The dorsal pathway is known to be highly responsive to images of tools, which convey visuomotor information (Chao and Martin, 2000; Lewis, 2006; Mruczek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: The reanalysis using only fMRI blocks with objects (and not tools) fully reproduced the analyses described above at the voxel-wise and ROI level.
source: Nevertheless, to ensure that the activation in the dorsal pathway was not solely a result of visuomotor associations, we reanalyzed the data of the two experiments using only the fMRI blocks in which objects (and not tools) were presented. Notwithstanding the loss of statistical power, the reanalysis fully reproduced the analyses described above at the voxel-wise and ROI level (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 upper panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 1-upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The results of the two experiments cannot be ascribed to the presence of tool stimuli that convey visuomotor associations.
source: The results of the two experiments, therefore, cannot be ascribed to the presence of tool stimuli that convey visuomotor associations, and, instead, bolster to the conclusion that posterior regions of dorsal cortex are responsive to the shape of the visual input.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the reanalysis.

claim: The two pathways followed a similar topographical organization with a posterior to anterior initial increase and then decrease in shape sensitivity.
source: First, the two pathways followed a similar topographical organization with a posterior to anterior initial increase and then decrease in shape sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the key findings.

claim: The representational structures of regions in the dorsal and ventral pathways were highly correlated with each other.
source: Second, the representational structures of regions in the dorsal and ventral pathways were highly correlated with each other.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the key findings.

claim: These findings challenge a strict functional dichotomy between the pathways and suggest a more distributed model of shape processing.
source: Together, these findings challenge the binary distinction between the two pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Shape sensitivity was not evident in the caudal parts of the ventral pathway and emerged in the rostral and lateral parts of the ventral pathway, reflecting the hierarchical nature of object processing.
source: Consistent with early investigations (e.g., Grill-Spector et al., 1998; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014; Lerner et al., 2001; Murray et al., 2002), shape sensitivity, was not evident in the caudal parts of the ventral pathway (i.e., early visual cortex) and emerged in the rostral and lateral parts of the ventral pathway, reflecting the hierarchical nature of object processing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: In the transition from high-level visual regions to even more anterior temporal regions, shape sensitivity was still present, albeit reduced.
source: However, in the transition from high-level visual regions (i.e., parahippocampal gyrus, fusiform gyrus) to even more anterior temporal regions, shape sensitivity was still present, albeit reduced (i.e., a flatter slope).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The anterior and medial regions of the temporal lobe may also play a role in object recognition.
source: Interestingly, in recent years, accumulating evidence has shown that the anterior and medial regions of the temporal lobe (i.e., perirhinal and entorhinal cortices) may also play a role in object recognition (Behrmann et al., 2016); for a review see Murray et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The results of the present investigation are compatible with the view that more anterior representations may be confined to high-level object properties and to memory-based representations, and less to shape and geometric information per se.
source: The results of the present investigation are compatible with the view that these more anterior representations may be confined to high-level object properties (such as conjunction of multiple features see, Barense et al., 2007; or familiarity, see Martin et al., 2013) and to memory-based representations, and less to shape and geometric information per se.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Shape sensitivity increased from early visual cortex to extrastriate cortex, reached its peak sensitivity in the posterior parietal cortex and then gradually decreased in more anterior regions in the dorsal pathway.
source: In particular, shape sensitivity increased from early visual cortex to extrastriate cortex, reached its peak sensitivity in the posterior parietal cortex and then gradually decreased in more anterior regions, closer to the central sulcus.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The similarity between the two pathways suggest that the topographical organization is constrained by similar factors, namely cortical distance from the visual cortex and connectivity to other cortical systems.
source: The similarity between the two pathways suggest that the topographical organization is constrained by similar factors, namely cortical distance from the visual cortex and connectivity to other cortical systems (i.e., the motor system in the dorsal pathway and semantic system in the ventral pathway).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The similarity in the large-scale organization of the two pathways was further confirmed by an RSA approach that revealed that the representational structure of regions in the posterior dorsal pathway was highly correlated with the representational structure of lateral-ventral ROI.
source: Finally, the similarity in the large-scale organization of the two pathways was further confirmed by an RSA approach that revealed that the representational structure of regions in the posterior dorsal pathway was highly correlated with the representational structure of lateral-ventral ROI.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Shape sensitivity was greater in the ventral than dorsal pathway, reflecting the centrality of this pathway in object perception.
source: Notably, despite these similarities, differences were also observed between the two pathways: shape sensitivity was greater in the ventral than dorsal pathway, reflecting the centrality of this pathway in object perception, and shape sensitivity reached its maximum values in more anterior regions of the ventral than dorsal pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Shape sensitivity reached its maximum values in more anterior regions of the ventral than dorsal pathway.
source: Notably, despite these similarities, differences were also observed between the two pathways: shape sensitivity was greater in the ventral than dorsal pathway, reflecting the centrality of this pathway in object perception, and shape sensitivity reached its maximum values in more anterior regions of the ventral than dorsal pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Pictures of tools activate regions in the dorsal pathway, even when no overt visuomotor task was required.
source: Some fMRI investigations have provided evidence that pictures of tools activate regions in the dorsal pathway (Chao and Martin, 2000; Valyear et al., 2007), even when no overt visuomotor task was required.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: More recent studies have documented dorsal activation for both 2D and 3D images, even when the stimuli do not have any visuomotor association and the task is not action-based.
source: More recent studies, however, have documented dorsal activation for both 2D and 3D images, even when the stimuli do not have any visuomotor association and the task is not action-based (Freud et al., 2015; Konen and Kastner, 2008; Zachariou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: When BOLD responses to tools were compared to non-tools (but graspable) objects, no difference was observed between the two categories in the posterior parts of the dorsal pathway, but greater activation was observed for tools than for objects in more anterior regions.
source: Moreover, when BOLD responses to tools were compared to non-tools (but graspable) objects, no difference was observed between the two categories in the posterior parts of the dorsal pathway, but greater activation was observed for tools than for objects in more anterior regions (Mruczek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Shape sensitivity within the dorsal pathway was found both for tools and non-tool objects.
source: In the current work, shape sensitivity within the dorsal pathway was found both for tools and non-tool objects.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The neural representation in the posterior regions of the dorsal pathway may reflect the processing of different shape cues such as the 3D status of the object and/or object elongation.
source: Together, these results suggest that the representations subserved by the posterior regions of the dorsal pathway are not limited to visuomotor associations evoked by the object. Instead, the neural representation may reflect the processing of different shape cues such as the 3D status of the object (Berryhill et al., 2009; Freud et al., 2017a; Konen and Kastner, 2008; Van Dromme et al., 2016) and/or object elongation (Chen et al., 2017; Fabbri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings and supported by citations.

claim: Posterior LOC was more correlated with a shape model than a category model.
source: For example, Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016 mapped the cortical sensitivity for a stimulus set in which shape and category (e.g., animals, musical instruments, tools) were dissociated. Similar to the present findings, posterior LOC was more correlated with a shape model than a category model.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The TOS was highly correlated with the shape model, and not with the category model.
source: In the dorsal pathway, the TOS, which corresponds to posterior ROIs in the probabilistic atlas used here, was also highly correlated with the shape model, and not with the category model.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Some anterior dorsal ROIs were more correlated with the category model, than the shape model.
source: Nevertheless, in this previous investigation, some anterior dorsal ROIs were more correlated with the category model, than the shape model.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Dorsal pathway representations were found to be highly sensitive to task properties.
source: As discussed below, dorsal pathway representations were found to be highly sensitive to task properties (Bracci et al., 2017) and therefore, the discrepancies between the present investigation and Bracci and Op de Beeck's findings might be related to the nature of the task: while Bracci and Op de Beeck asked participants to compare the real-size of preceding images (encouraging object-based processing), in the present investigation, we deliberately avoided explicit processing of the stimuli and had participants complete an orthogonal fixation-based task.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Along the dorsal pathway a decrease in shape sensitivity was found for the diffeomorphic manipulation, compared with the results obtained from the box scrambling experiment.
source: In contrast to the inferior surface of the ventral pathway, along the dorsal pathway a decrease in shape sensitivity was found for this manipulation, compared with the results obtained from the box scrambling experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Dorsal pathway representations are tied to the presence of a single coherent shape, even if it is not identifiable as a familiar object and lacks important visual properties.
source: Hence, our results suggest that dorsal pathway representations are tied to the presence of a single coherent shape, even if it is not identifiable as a familiar object and lacks important visual properties.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The residual perceptual abilities of patients with visual agnosia are consistent with the interpretation that dorsal representations can support sensitivity to particular attributes but cannot support intact recognition abilities.
source: The residual perceptual abilities of patients with visual agnosia are consistent with such interpretation. In particular, the dissociable dorsal representations can support sensitivity to particular attributes (such as the 3D structure of an object) but cannot support intact recognition abilities (Freud et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: There was a correlation between recognition abilities and fMRI shape sensitivity in the posterior part of the dorsal pathway, even when the correlation of these variables with scrambling levels was partialled out.
source: Here, we provide novel evidence for a correlation between recognition abilities and fMRI shape sensitivity in the posterior part of the dorsal pathway, even when the correlation of these variables with scrambling levels was partialled out.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The correlations between fMRI activation and behavioral performance point to a plausible functional contribution of the dorsal pathway to object perception.
source: Despite the inability to infer causality from those correlations, they extend seminal findings that found correlations between perceptual performance and fMRI activation in different regions of the ventral pathway (Grill-Spector et al., 2000) and point to a plausible functional contribution of the dorsal pathway to object perception.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings and supported by a citation.

claim: A patient with an occipitoparietal lesion was impaired in the perception of objects defined by monocular and binocular cues.
source: Consistent with this suggestion, a patient with an occipitoparietal lesion was impaired in the perception of objects defined by monocular and binocular cues (Berryhill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Recent studies, using TMS in humans and reversible deactivation in non-human primates, have successfully established a causal relationship between the dorsal activation and perceptual classification.
source: Moreover, recent studies, using TMS in humans and reversible deactivation in non-human primates, have successfully established a causal relationship between the dorsal activation and perceptual classification (Van Dromme et al., 2016; Zachariou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The dorsal pathway appears not to be sufficient to support intact perception and object recognition, and the ventral pathway remains more central to this function.
source: Notably, as evident from visual agnosia patients and from the results of the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, the dorsal pathway appears not to be sufficient to support intact perception and object recognition, and the ventral pathway remains more central to this function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: There was a decrease in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the dorsal pathway, in both univariate and multivariate analyses.
source: In both experiments reported here, there was a decrease in shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the dorsal pathway, in both univariate and multivariate analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The aIPS is a region associated with computations related to the representations of objects in the context of visuomotor tasks.
source: This was particularly evident in the aIPS, a region associated with computations related to the representations of objects in the context of visuomotor tasks (Culham et al., 2003; for a recent review see, Gallivan and Culham, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Several other neuroimaging investigations in humans and electrophysiological studies non-human primates have revealed shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the IPS.
source: However, several other neuroimaging investigations in humans and electrophysiological studies non-human primates have revealed shape sensitivity in the anterior parts of the IPS (Durand et al., 2007; Freud et al., 2017b; Janssen et al., 2000; Orban, 2011; Theys et al., 2013; Theys et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The nature of the task modulates shape sensitivity in the dorsal pathway.
source: This apparent contradiction raises the possibility that the nature of the task modulates shape sensitivity in the dorsal pathway, and, indeed, a recent study found that the aIPS coded object shape and elongation during grasping but not during passive viewing (Fabbri et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Task demands were found to modulate the nature of representations in other regions of the dorsal pathway, under perceptual tasks.
source: Moreover, task demands were found to modulate the nature of representations in other regions of the dorsal pathway, under perceptual (rather than visuomotor) tasks, further suggesting that dorsal pathway representations might be sensitive to tasks demands (Bracci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: The ventral pathway is less affected by task demands.
source: Notably, in contrast to these findings, a recent study revealed that the ventral pathway is less affected by task demands (Bugatus et al., 2017), revealing potential differences in the way task modulates the representations in the two pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Posterior extrastriate regions of the dorsal pathway are highly sensitive to shape information (but less to object identity).
source: The present study uncovered novel evidence for the nature of shape representations along the dorsal pathway and its similarity to representations along the ventral pathway. In two fMRI experiments, using a variety of analytical approaches, we found that posterior extrastriate regions of the dorsal pathway are highly sensitive to shape information (but less to object identity), that the magnitude of their activation is correlated with perceptual behaviors and that in some regions, the representations derived are highly similar to those in some regions of ventral cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The magnitude of activation in posterior extrastriate regions of the dorsal pathway is correlated with perceptual behaviors.
source: The present study uncovered novel evidence for the nature of shape representations along the dorsal pathway and its similarity to representations along the ventral pathway. In two fMRI experiments, using a variety of analytical approaches, we found that posterior extrastriate regions of the dorsal pathway are highly sensitive to shape information (but less to object identity), that the magnitude of their activation is correlated with perceptual behaviors and that in some regions, the representations derived are highly similar to those in some regions of ventral cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: In some regions of the dorsal pathway, the representations derived are highly similar to those in some regions of ventral cortex.
source: The present study uncovered novel evidence for the nature of shape representations along the dorsal pathway and its similarity to representations along the ventral pathway. In two fMRI experiments, using a variety of analytical approaches, we found that posterior extrastriate regions of the dorsal pathway are highly sensitive to shape information (but less to object identity), that the magnitude of their activation is correlated with perceptual behaviors and that in some regions, the representations derived are highly similar to those in some regions of ventral cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Sensitivity to shape information decreases in anterior regions of the dorsal pathway reflecting a gradual shift from representation-for-perception to representation-for action.
source: This sensitivity decreases in anterior regions of the dorsal pathway reflecting a gradual shift from representation-for-perception to representation-for action, leading to the conclusion that there is a representational continuum from more posterior areas tuned to visual properties of the objects in the input to more anterior areas tuned to motor aspects of the observed objects.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: There is a representational continuum from more posterior areas tuned to visual properties of the objects in the input to more anterior areas tuned to motor aspects of the observed objects.
source: This sensitivity decreases in anterior regions of the dorsal pathway reflecting a gradual shift from representation-for-perception to representation-for action, leading to the conclusion that there is a representational continuum from more posterior areas tuned to visual properties of the objects in the input to more anterior areas tuned to motor aspects of the observed objects.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Twenty-two right-handed participants participated in the study.
source: Twenty-two right-handed participants (box scrambling experiment: Eleven participants, nine males; mean age: 31, range: 19–46 years, diffeomorphic scrambling experiment: Eleven participants, five males; mean age: 25, range: 19–46 years).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The data obtained from two additional participants were not analyzed due to excessive head movements during multiple scans.
source: The data obtained from two additional participants were not analyzed due to excessive head movements (>3 mm) during multiple scans.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and were financially compensated for their participation.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Informed consent was obtained prior to the study.
source: Informed consent was obtained prior to the study.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Carnegie Mellon University.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Carnegie Mellon University.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Stimuli in the box scrambling experiment were 160 grayscale pictures of everyday objects and tools downloaded from The Bank of Standardized Stimuli.
source: Stimuli were 160 grayscale pictures of everyday objects (80 pictures) and tools (80 pictures) downloaded from The Bank of Standardized Stimuli (BOSS) (Brodeur et al., 2010; Brodeur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Each image in the box scrambling experiment was divided into 4, 16, 64 and 256 squares that were randomly rearranged, resulting in five levels of scrambling.
source: Each image was divided into 4, 16, 64 and 256 squares that were randomly rearranged, resulting in five levels of scrambling (Figure 1) (most scrambled to intact - S4, S3, S2, S1 and Full).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Stimuli in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment were 320 grayscale pictures of everyday objects and tools downloaded from The Bank of Standardized Stimuli.
source: Stimuli were 320 grayscale pictures of everyday objects (160 pictures) and tools (160 pictures) downloaded from The Bank of Standardized Stimuli (BOSS) (Brodeur et al., 2010; 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: In the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, only one version of each picture was presented to a particular participant to ensure that sensitivity to object shape was not modulated by within-experiment priming or adaptation.
source: In contrast to the box scrambling experiment, only one version of each picture was presented to a particular participant (counterbalanced across participants) to ensure that sensitivity to object shape was not modulated by within-experiment priming or adaptation.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For each object in the diffeomorphic scrambling experiment, five versions were created.
source: For each object, five versions were created (no distortion, one distortion step, two distortion steps, four distortion steps and eight distortion steps, distortion level = 80; Matlab function was provided by Stojanoski and Cusack, Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pixel similarity analysis revealed greater similarity between the intact images and distorted images in diffeomorphic scrambling experiment compared with box scrambling experiment.
source: This analysis revealed greater similarity (higher values) between the intact images and distorted images in diffeomorphic scrambling experiment compared with box scrambling experiment (box scrambling: 0.7 ± 0.02; diffeomorphic scrambling: 0.87 ± 0.03).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Image entropy analysis showed greater entropy for the box scrambling stimuli.
source: These analyses showed greater entropy and lower homogeneity for the box scrambling stimuli (Image entropy: box scrambling: 1.07 ± 0.07; diffeomorphic scrambling: 1.02 ± 0.13; Image homogeneity: box scrambling: 0.98 ± 0.007; diffeomorphic scrambling: 0.99 ± 0.005)
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Image homogeneity analysis showed lower homogeneity for the box scrambling stimuli.
source: These analyses showed greater entropy and lower homogeneity for the box scrambling stimuli (Image entropy: box scrambling: 1.07 ± 0.07; diffeomorphic scrambling: 1.02 ± 0.13; Image homogeneity: box scrambling: 0.98 ± 0.007; diffeomorphic scrambling: 0.99 ± 0.005)
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The convex hull analysis confirmed that shape properties were distorted even by the diffeomorphic images, but were still better preserved for these images compared with the box-scrambled images across all levels of scrambling.
source: As with the other algorithms, this procedure confirmed that shape properties were distorted even by the diffeomorphic images, but were still better preserved for these images compared with the box-scrambled images across all levels of scrambling (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Participants were scanned in a Siemens Verio 3-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging scanner with a 32-channels coil at Carnegie Mellon University.
source: Participants were scanned in a Siemens Verio 3-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging scanner with a 32-channels coil at Carnegie Mellon University.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: A structural scan was acquired using a T1-weighted protocol that included 176 sagittal slices.
source: A structural scan was acquired using a T1-weighted protocol that included 176 sagittal slices (1 mm thickness, in-plane resolution = 1 mm, matrix = 256×256, repetition time = 2300 ms, echo time = 1.97 ms, inversion time = 900 ms, flip angle = 9 ̊).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Functional images based on the blood oxygenation level-dependent signal were acquired with a gradient-echo, echoplanar imaging sequence.
source: Functional images based on the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal were acquired with a gradient-echo, echoplanar imaging sequence (TR = 1.5 s, TE = 30 ms, flip angle 73 ̊).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: To achieve full coverage of both visual pathways, 43 axial slices were acquired in eight runs of 227 volumes each.
source: To achieve full coverage of both visual pathways, 43 axial slices (slice thickness = 3 mm, gap = 0 mm, in-plane resolution = 3 mm) were acquired in eight runs of 227 volumes each (such that each run lasted 5 min, 40.5 s).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Participants were instructed to fixate on the cross in the center of the display during the fMRI experiment.
source: Participants were instructed to fixate on the cross in the center of the display.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: To maintain attention throughout the scan, participants were required to indicate, via a button press, when the color of the fixation cross changed from black to red.
source: To maintain attention throughout the scan, participants were required to indicate, via a button press, when the color of the fixation cross changed from black to red.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Participants returned 2–3 weeks after completing the fMRI experiment for the behavioral object recognition test.
source: Participants returned 2–3 weeks after completing the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: In the behavioral object recognition test, participants were shown the same stimuli they had viewed in the scanner and were instructed to name aloud each stimulus.
source: Seated 50 cm in front of a computer screen in a darkened room, they were shown the same stimuli they had viewed in the scanner and were instructed to name aloud each stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: fMRI raw data are available at https://doi.org/10.1184/R1/c.3889873.v1.
source: fMRI raw data are available at https://doi.org/10.1184/R1/c.3889873.v1 and were processed using BrainVoyager 20.2 software (Brain Innovation, Maastricht, Netherlands; RRID:SCR_013057), MRIcron (RRID:SCR_002403), complementary in-house software written in Matlab (The MathWorks, Inc, Natick, MA, USA; RRID:SCR_001622; see source code) and R Development Core Team (2009).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Preprocessing included 3D-motion correction and filtering of low temporal frequencies.
source: Preprocessing included 3D-motion correction and filtering of low temporal frequencies (cutoff frequency of 2 cycles per run).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: No spatial smoothing was applied to allow the voxel-wise analysis.
source: No spatial smoothing was applied to allow the voxel-wise analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All scans were transformed to Montreal Neurological Institute space.
source: All scans were transformed to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space (Fonov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: A group-level mask of all visually selective voxels was generated by performing a random-effects general linear model analysis across all 22 participants.
source: A group-level mask of all visually selective voxels was generated by performing a random-effects general linear model (GLM) analysis across all 22 participants.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: If a voxel was reliably responsive to any of the five conditions relative to fixation, it was included in the mask.
source: If a voxel was reliably responsive to any of these conditions (q < 0.05, false-discovery rate (FDR)-corrected, Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) relative to fixation, it was included in the mask, which was then applied in the individual subject analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All voxels superior to the calcarine sulcus were considered part of the dorsal pathway, and all the voxels inferior to the calcarine sulcus were considered part of the ventral pathway.
source: All voxels superior to the calcarine sulcus were considered part of the dorsal pathway, and all the voxels inferior to the calcarine sulcus were considered part of the ventral pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The voxel-wise approach yielded 941 functional voxels in the right dorsal pathway, 1155 functional voxels in the left dorsal pathway, 1793 functional voxels in the right ventral pathway and 1736 functional voxels in the left ventral pathway.
source: This approach yielded the following distribution: right dorsal pathway (941 functional voxels), left dorsal pathway (1155 functional voxels), right ventral pathway (1793 functional voxels) and left ventral pathway (1736 functional voxels).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For each participant, a voxel-wise GLM was conducted and a beta value for each of the five conditions was calculated.
source: For each participant, a voxel-wise GLM was conducted and a beta value for each of the five conditions was calculated.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The slope of activation as a function of scrambling level was calculated for each voxel to assess shape sensitivity.
source: Next, to assess shape sensitivity, the slope of activation (beta values) as a function of scrambling level was calculated for each voxel.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: A positive slope reflects an increase in activation as the level of scrambling decreases, and therefore reflects greater shape sensitivity.
source: A positive slope reflects an increase in activation as the level of scrambling decreases (from S4 to intact), and therefore reflects greater shape sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: A negative slope represents a decrease in activation as the level of scrambling decreases, and may reflect greater sensitivity to local elements and edges.
source: A negative slope represents a decrease in activation as the level of scrambling decreases, and, as such, may reflect greater sensitivity to local elements and edges, which are more frequent in increasingly distorted images (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: A piecewise regression analysis was conducted separately for each participant, pathway and hemisphere.
source: Since an initial inspection showed that the topographical organization might not be linear, we conducted a piecewise regression analysis separately for each participant, pathway and hemisphere, using the shape language modelling (SLM) toolbox available in Matlab.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The number of segments in the piecewise regression was limited to two to avoid overfitting of the data.
source: To avoid overfitting of the data, we limited the number of segments to two, and the segmentation point was automatically derived to maximize the R2.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: In each pathway, the piecewise linear regression robustly increased the R2 compared with a simple linear regression.
source: Notably, in each pathway, the piecewise linear regression robustly increased the R2 was compared with a R2 obtained from a simple linear regression (ps < 0.005, see Table 1), suggesting that the former provides a better fit to the data than a one-component linear model.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section and shown in Table 1.

claim: ROIs were defined based on a probabilistic atlas.
source: We defined ROIs based on a probabilistic atlas (Wang et al., 2015) that includes regions along the ventral and the dorsal visual pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The aIPS ROI was defined based on a meta-analysis.
source: Since we were also interested in more anterior parts of the dorsal pathway, we defined the anterior intraparietal sulcus (aIPS) bilaterally by selecting voxels located in the vicinity of the junction of the intraparietal sulcus and the post-central sulcus based on coordinates extracted from Neurosynth (http://neurosynth.org/) using the search term 'Grasping' (Hutchison and Gallivan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For early visual ROIs, a more restricted ROI was defined at the posterior part of the original ROIs to capture foveal representation.
source: Finally, since our stimuli were always presented at the center of the visual field, for early visual ROIs (V1v, V2v, V3v, V1d, V2d, V3d), we defined a more restricted ROI (5 mm sphere) at the posterior part of the original ROIs as defined in the probabilistic atlas, in order to capture foveal representation (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: For each ROI, beta weights for each of the five conditions were calculated, and the linear slope between the beta weights was extracted and served as a measure of shape sensitivity of that ROI.
source: For each ROI, beta weights for each of the five conditions were calculated, and then, as with the voxel-wise analysis, the linear slope between the beta weights was extracted and served as a measure of shape sensitivity of that ROI.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Beta weights from the different ROIs were extracted separately for each run and condition for the RSA.
source: To do so, beta weights from the different ROIs were extracted separately for each run and condition (8 runs x 5 conditions = 40) and the runs were separated into two sets with similar visual information contained in each set.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The correlations between all the odd and even runs were extracted resulting in an asymmetric correlation matrix for the RSA.
source: The correlations between all the odd and even runs were extracted resulting in an asymmetric correlation matrix (20 × 20).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The Spearman correlation between the correlation matrix of each ROI and a shape model correlation matrix was computed for the RSA.
source: To examine whether shape information was similarly encoded by different ROIs, we computed the Spearman correlation between the correlation matrix of each ROI and a shape model correlation matrix (see Figures 4 and 5) that proposes that representations of images will be more similar to each other if they possess similar levels of shape information.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Correlation values were Fisher transformed to permit further statistical comparisons in the RSA.
source: These correlation values were Fisher transformed to permit further statistical comparisons.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: One-sample t-test was used to determine whether a specific ROI conveys shape information in the RSA.
source: One-sample t-test (p<0.05, FDR corrected) was used to determine whether a specific ROI conveys shape information (r > 0).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The reliability index was calculated by correlating the correlation matrix of each subject in each ROI with the average matrix obtained from all other subjects.
source: To estimate the upper limit of the correlation given the noise in the data, we calculated reliability for each ROI (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016). The correlation matrix of each subject in each ROI was correlated with the average matrix obtained from all other subjects.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The pattern of activation in each ROI was correlated with the activation pattern of all other ROIs for the second-level RSA.
source: Finally, the pattern of activation in each ROI was correlated with the activation pattern of all other ROIs.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Multi-Dimensional Scaling approach was utilized to visualize the similarity of the response patterns of the different ROIs.
source: To visualize the similarity of the response patterns of the different ROIs, we averaged the correlation matrices of all the participants and utilized the Multi-Dimensional Scaling approach (MDS, 'mdscale' Matlab command).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The fMRI data were divided into two datasets for the correlation with object recognition analysis.
source: The univariate analyses described above included just five levels (scrambling), limiting the ability to calculate a reliable correlation between participants' BOLD response and object recognition abilities. We therefore divided the fMRI data into two datasets, in which different objects were presented, and we separated the data from the tools and objects categories.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: This procedure yielded 20 beta weights for each ROI for the correlation with object recognition analysis.
source: This procedure yielded 20 beta weights for each ROI.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Partial correlations between behavioral performance and fMRI signal were computed, controlling for the correlation of these two variables with the level of scrambling.
source: Partial correlations between behavioral performance and fMRI signal were computed, controlling for the correlation of these two variables with the level of scrambling.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.
